derby.desk_intro:
Welcome to the Gullhaven Fishing Derby!
You get {n} Tidelumens, one per cast.

Today's featured fish: {featured}.
Catch one for x{mult} points. Enter?
derby.desk_busy:
Still {n} Tidelumens in your pouch,
and {score} points so far. Keep casting!
derby.turn_in_early:
You've still got {n} Tidelumens.
Turn in your haul now anyway?
derby.start:
The derby's on! The town clock stops
until you turn in. No rush at all.
derby.no_crystal:
No Tidelumens left to cast.
Take your haul to the weigh-in scale.
derby.catch:
Onto the scale: {species}, {kg} kg.
That's {points} points!
derby.record:
The needle bangs the end of the scale.
That's a record-size catch!
derby.out:
That was your last Tidelumen.
Time for the weigh-in!
derby.leave_ask:
Leave the lagoon now and the run is
forfeit. Quit the derby?
derby.forfeit:
Run forfeit. The haul slips back
into the lagoon with a splash.
derby.scale_idle:
The weigh-in scale, wet with spray.
Your best derby score: {best}.
derby.turn_in:
The clerk adds it all up.
Final score: {score}!

That's a {tier}-tier haul!
Here's your prize.

Lantern festival's on in Lanternport.
Your prize would look good in it.
derby.no_tier:
The clerk adds it all up.
Final score: {score}.

Not enough for a prize this time.
The lagoon will be here tomorrow.
derby.new_best:
A new best score! The clerk chalks
it up on the board by the desk.
derby.keeper:
Your heaviest catch, {species}
({kg} kg), is coming home with you!

Last swimmer before the harbour.
Nobody gets past me dry.

Kelp grows on the walls in here. The
wind sings through it on a high tide.

I came for a week. That was nine
years ago. Lovely acoustics.

Had a dream the sea was asking me
something. Couldn't hear the end.

Sat up the rest of the night. Felt
like I owed somebody an answer.

Found a wet print on the slip one
morning. Big. Pointing inland.

Tide took it by noon. Probably
nothing. I didn't go looking.

Gull bones, all down the walls. Old
nests. Very old. Nothing to fear.

Mostly. Mind the drip on the left.
It's been aiming at me for years.

Come back soon. The fish are

My great-gran Bryn came in empty one
spring tide. Said she let it go.

Longer than the harbour, she said,
with a light on its brow.

Like a lantern somebody forgot
to put out. It looked at her.

The way a dog looks at a door. Then
it swam for the old river mouth.

Nobody believed her. Next year the
river ran lower. Then lower again.

So we fish for Bryn's fish and never
expect it. Big enough to let go.
